meta.title: MeCoLog: Meta-contrastive learning for cross-system few-shot log-based anomaly detection

p1-s1.text: RESEARCH ARTICLE MeCoLog: Meta-contrastive learning for crosssystem few-shot log-based anomaly detection

p1-s2.text: Manh Tuan Nguyen , Tuan Phong Tran, Le Dinh Trang Dang, Van Loi Cao *

p1-s3.text: Institute of Information and Communication Technology, Le Quy Don Technical University,‌ Hanoi, ‌Vietnam

p1-s6.text: System logs are widely used for monitoring system reliability and detecting abnormal behaviors in large-scale computing infrastructures.

p1-s7.text: While deep learning has significantly advanced log anomaly detection, most existing methods are confined to in-domain scenarios, relying heavily on abundant system-specific historical data.

p1-s8.text: Consequently, they struggle to monitor newly deployed systems where log data and anomaly labels are severely scarce.

p1-s9.text: Achieving robust cross-system log anomaly detection remains a challenge due to inherent domain gaps, including completely different logging structures, continuously evolving templates and severe Out-Of-Vocabulary issues.

p1-s10.text: To bridge these gaps, we propose MeCoLog, a Meta- Contrastive learning method for cross-system log anomaly detection.

p1-s11.text: First, a Hybrid Parameter Embedding is introduced to encode type, value, and key information to handle diverse vocabularies.

p1-s12.text: These embeddings are integrated into the model via a Gated Key Injection mechanism and Rotary Position Embedding.

p1-s13.text: These allow the model to capture both event relevance and execution flow.

p1-s14.text: Second, we design an Asymmetric Prototype Contrastive Learning objective.

p1-s15.text: This method aligns normal behaviors across different systems while strictly isolating anomalies.

p1-s24.text: Extensive experiments on multiple public log datasets (HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, Hadoop and AIT-LDS v2.0) demonstrate that MeCoLog consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under few-shot cross-system settings, offering a robust and highly transferable solution for real-world log anomaly detection.

p1-s30.text: Modern large-scale computing infrastructures generate massive volumes of system logs.

p1-s31.text: These infrastructures include cloud platforms, distributed storage systems, and microservice-based services.

p1-s32.text: The logs capture runtime events, execution states, resource usage, warnings, and failures.

p1-s33.text: They serve as critical evidence for system monitoring, fault diagnosis, and security analytics [1–4].

p2-s2.text: Abnormal log patterns often provide early indicators of service disruption, misconfiguration, malicious activity and ongoing attacks [3,5,6].

p2-s3.text: Modern infrastructures continue to grow in scale and complexity.

p2-s4.text: As a result, manual inspection of logs becomes impractical, making it increasingly challenging to effectively monitor and analyze log data for potential security threats.

p2-s5.text: This trend has motivated the development of automated log anomaly detection techniques [3].

p2-s9.text: Early methods for log anomaly detection relied on handcrafted rules or statistical analysis of event frequencies [1,7].

p2-s10.text: More recently, deep learning approaches have advanced the field.

p2-s11.text: These approaches learn sequence representations directly from log data.

p2-s12.text: Sequence models such as LSTM and Transformer architectures capture temporal dependencies among log events [5,6,8].

p2-s13.text: Representation-learning methods employ pretrained language models and contextual embeddings [3,9].

p2-s14.text: These methods achieve strong performance within individual systems.

p2-s15.text: However, their effectiveness often tends to diminish when applied to new environments [10,11].

p2-s16.text: Full retraining for every newly monitored system is often infeasible due to the prohibitive cost of collecting labeled anomalies.

p2-s17.text: To address this, cross-system log anomaly detection aims to leverage knowledge extracted from previously observed environments to secure new ones.

p2-s18.text: This approach enables rapid adaptation to target systems using only a minimal number of labeled samples [10,12,13].

p2-s19.text: This setting is practically important because target systems often provide only limited labeled data.

p2-s20.text: Such efficiency is essential for defenders to maintain robust performance even under significant system shifts.

p2-s21.text: Cross-system log anomaly detection presents several challenges.

p2-s23.text: A newly monitored target system may provide only a handful of labeled examples for calibration.

p2-s24.text: Standard supervised methods [9] fail in this regime because they require large annotated datasets.

p2-s25.text: Similarly, semi-supervised methods are sensitive to distributional drift and cannot effectively leverage the few available anomaly labels [11,14,15].

p2-s26.text: Therefore, rapid and data-efficient adaptation to new systems requires an inductive learning strategy optimized for few-shot generalization.

p2-s27.text: Second, the domain gap across systems appears in both log structure and parameter semantics.

p2-s28.text: Different systems use different vocabularies, template structures, logging styles, abbreviations, and parameter distributions [10–12].

p2-s29.text: As a result, even similar events, such as failed authentication or disk write errors, may be described with different words and patterns.

p2-s30.text: Standard log parsers such as Drain [7] normalize logs by replacing variable fields with generic wildcards.

p2-s31.text: Although this reduces vocabulary variation, it also removes parameter information and can create Out-Of- Vocabulary (OOV) issues when templates from a new system are encountered.

p2-s32.text: This limits the transferability of methods that rely on system-specific token vocabularies.

p2-s33.text: In addition, variable parameters often contain important anomaly evidence, such as abnormal resource values, unusual IP addresses, file paths, node identifiers, or system states [9,16].

p2-s34.text: These signals are often more system-independent than templates, making them especially useful for cross-system transfer.

p3-s3.text: Third, current methods lack an effective discriminative mechanism that accounts for the inherent distribution asymmetry between normal and anomalous log sequences.

p3-s4.text: Normal operational behaviors usually exhibit stable, recurring patterns that are largely consistent across different systems [5,17].

p3-s5.text: In contrast, anomalies are fundamentally different.

p3-s6.text: They arise from unpredictable sources such as misconfigurations, hardware faults, or cyber attacks.

p3-s7.text: This makes them inherently diverse and structurally arbitrary.

p3-s8.text: Existing detection objectives often overlook this geometric distinction.

p3-s9.text: They either assume a single closed-loop boundary for all data or force diverse anomalies into a single artificial cluster.

p3-s10.text: Based on these fundamental challenges, this study aims to address the following three research questions:

p3-s11.text: • RQ1 (Knowledge Transfer): How can a model effectively transfer diagnostic knowledge from a source system to a target system when only a minimal number of labeled samples are available?

p3-s12.text: • RQ2 (Feature Extraction): How can semantic templates and heterogeneous log parameters be integrated into a unified representation that remains robust across diverse system environments?

p3-s13.text: • RQ3 (Representation Learning): How can the model leverage the natural structure of log data to improve cross-system transferability?

p3-s14.text: To address the cross-system knowledge transfer challenge (RQ1), we propose MeCoLog (Meta-Contrastive Learning for Log Anomaly Detection).

p3-s15.text: This method formulates the detection task as an episodic few-shot learning problem.

p3-s16.text: This approach addresses both label scarcity and domain gap by training the model on a source system and adapting it to a new target system using only a small labeled support set, without any retraining.

p3-s17.text: To optimize feature extraction from heterogeneous log data (RQ2), we integrate structured parameter information directly into log sequence embeddings through a Hybrid Parameters Embedding approach.

p3-s18.text: This mechanism preserves the full semantic content of log messages by applying specialized encoding branches for different parameter types.

p3-s19.text: These embeddings are then fused into the Transformer attention mechanism via our proposed Gated Key Injection (GKI) mechanism, allowing parameter context to selectively modulate inter-event relevance.

p3-s20.text: Furthermore, relative sequential dependencies are captured through Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [18], ensuring the encoder remains sensitive to the execution flow rather than absolute event positions.

p3-s21.text: To address the challenge of representation learning (RQ3), we introduce an Asymmetric Prototype Contrastive Loss (APCL).

p3-s22.text: This objective is based on the observation that normal behaviors usually reflect stable, system-agnostic operational states.

p3-s23.text: Consequently, they serve as the primary anchor for knowledge transfer.

p3-s24.text: In contrast, anomalous behaviors are far more heterogeneous and should not be forced into a single, artificial cluster.

p3-s25.text: Our asymmetric design therefore encourages normal samples from diverse systems to form compact, transferable clusters that serve as a reliable

p4-s3.text: Combined with metric-based meta-learning, this objective shapes a representation space.

p4-s4.text: By leveraging the natural stability of normal data, it supports robust cross-system transfer under few-shot conditions.

p4-s5.text: The main contributions of this work are as follows:

p4-s6.text: • We propose MeCoLog, a meta-learning method that formulates cross-system log anomaly detection as an episodic fewshot problem.

p4-s7.text: This enables rapid, training-free adaptation to new target systems using only a minimal labeled support set.

p4-s8.text: • We design a Hybrid Parameter Embedding that encodes log parameters in a domain-agnostic manner, resolving crosssystem OOV issues.

p4-s9.text: These features are integrated via a Gated Key Injection (GKI) mechanism and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), allowing the model to detect both semantic and sequential anomalies within a unified attention computation.

p4-s10.text: • We introduce an Asymmetric Prototype Contrastive Loss (APCL) that leverages the natural geometry of log data.

p4-s11.text: By encouraging compact clusters for normal patterns and allowing diverse dispersion for anomalies, APCL yields a representation space that is both highly transferable and discriminative under few-shot conditions.

p4-s12.text: • We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets, including HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, and AIT- LDS.

p4-s13.text: The results demonstrate that MeCoLog significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in few-shot crosssystem scenarios, maintaining high detection accuracy and operational efficiency.

p4-s14.text: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work and provides motivation.

p4-s15.text: Section 3 presents the MeCoLog method in detail.

p4-s16.text: Section 4 reports experimental setup and results.

p4-s17.text: Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

p4-s20.text: Log anomaly detection typically follows a four-stage pipeline: log collection, log parsing, feature extraction, and anomaly detection [2,3,19].

p4-s21.text: Raw log records encoding execution events are transformed by a log parser (e.g., Drain [7], Spell [20], or UniParser [21]) into structured templates by replacing variable fields with wildcards.

p4-s22.text: The resulting template sequences are encoded into numerical representations, such as event count vectors or ordered key sequences grouped by windows [1,5], before being passed to the detection model.

p4-s23.text: These models differ substantially in their supervision assumptions, spanning supervised approaches (e.g., LogRobust [9]), semi-supervised methods that model normal execution paths (e.g., DeepLog [5], LogAnomaly [6], LogBERT [8]), and unsupervised clustering techniques (e.g., LogCluster [22], NeuralLog [16]).

p4-s24.text: Despite their efficacy, all three paradigms are fundamentally restricted to single-system settings and degrade substantially under cross-system deployment due to shifting logging behaviors [10–12].

p4-s25.text: To capture anomalies invisible to template-only configurations, a parallel line of work explicitly integrates parameter information into log representations.

p4-s26.text: HitAnomaly [23] utilizes separate Transformer encoders for templates and parameters, while Chai et al. [24] preserve parameter semantics within a BERT framework.

p4-s27.text: Similarly, LogFormer [25] injects character-level parameter encodings as scalar attention biases.

p4-s28.text: Crucially, while these methods confirm the value of parameter-aware representations, they remain inherently tied to source-system vocabularies or apply biases uniformly without distinguishing template keywords from parameters.

p4-s29.text: Furthermore, their multi-stage pipelines are not designed for the label-scarce, cross-system regime that MeCoLog targets.

p4-s31.text: Cross-system log anomaly detection aims to deploy models on unseen target domains with minimal supervision by leveraging knowledge from source systems [10,12,13].

p4-s32.text: Existing strategies explore adversarial domain adaptation to align

p5-s1.text: global feature distributions (LogTransfer [10]), unsupervised nearest-neighbor scoring (Han et al. [12]), structural graph Transformers (LogGT [11]), and episodic meta-learning for rapid adaptation (MetaLog [13]).

p5-s2.text: Despite these advancements, cross-system deployment faces a fundamental linguistic and structural gap driven by disparate logging libraries, template formats, and parameter distributions.

p5-s3.text: Traditional parsing discards crucial systemagnostic operational semantics (e.g., numerical resource metrics or node identifiers) through wildcard substitution, eliminating anchors that could establish cross-system correspondence.

p5-s4.text: Even operationally identical behaviors are expressed through entirely different structures.

p5-s5.text: As quantified in Fig 2, while dense semantic encoders like SBERT [26] may suggest moderate proximity (0.62–0.75) via coarse geometric clustering of technical terms, strict lexical measures like the Word­ Net Lemma Jaccard similarity reveal near-total disjointedness (0.07–0.25).

p5-s6.text: Models anchored to source-specific surface tokens lack the reliable lexical footing necessary to generalize, resulting in poor performance under domain shifts.

p5-s7.text: Furthermore, existing cross-system paradigms fail to account for the asymmetric geometry of normal versus anomalous behaviors under few-shot constraints.

p5-s8.text: In real-world deployments, anomalies are severely underrepresented, often comprising less than one percent of log streams [3].

p5-s9.text: Consequently, a target support set of a few labeled instances cannot cover the full diversity of arbitrary system failures.

p5-s10.text: As visualized in Fig 3, while normal behaviors form compact, stable clusters, anomalies exhibit a high degree of dispersion and unpredictable structural shapes.

p5-s11.text: Contrastive objectives [14,27] that enforce uniform compactness across all classes are therefore ill-suited to this domain.

p5-s12.text: While metric-based meta-learning networks [28,29] optimize for fast adaptation with sparse data, they must be coupled with an embedding space that respects this natural asymmetry.

p5-s13.text: MeCoLog directly addresses these compounding limitations by fusing hybrid parameter encoding with an asymmetric contrastive learning objective within an episodic meta-learning framework.

p5-s16.text: We propose MeCoLog, a metric-based meta-learning method for cross-system log anomaly detection.

p5-s17.text: The method addresses the two principal challenges of cross-system deployment: label scarcity in the target system and the domain gap between heterogeneous logging environments.

p5-s18.text: The overall pipeline proceeds as follows.

p5-s19.text: Raw log sequences are first parsed into structured representations consisting of a template and a set of typed parameters.

p5-s20.text: For each log event, type-specific parameter embeddings are constructed and aggregated into a single parameter embedding.

p6-s9.text: Standard log parsers replace variable parameters with wildcards, discarding critical operational context such as resource identifiers, numerical values, system states, and path information [7].

p6-s10.text: This also creates cross-system incompatibility because value vocabularies differ between systems.

p6-s11.text: We address both issues by constructing type-specific parameter embeddings that encode operational semantics in a domain-agnostic manner.

p6-s12.text: These embeddings are then injected into the Transformer encoder jointly with relative positional information.

p6-s16.text: For each log event, we extract parameters using regular expressions and represent them as tuples (k, v, τ), where k is the key, v is the value, and τ is the type.

p6-s17.text: The type τ is inferred from predefined patterns and belongs to the set {NUM, IP, HEX, PATH, STR}.

p6-s18.text: If a parameter appears in explicit key-value form (e.g., user = root), the key is extracted directly; otherwise, a positional key k = POSj is assigned according to its order in the line.

p6-s19.text: The set of positional keys is fixed and shared across all datasets.

p6-s20.text: Value embeddings are computed differently according to type to preserve operational semantics without relying on dataset-specific vocabularies.

p6-s21.text: For categorical strings (τ ∈{STR, PATH}), we apply a character-level CNN encoder: the value is tokenized into characters, embedded, passed through 1D convolution with ReLU activation, and max-pooled.

p6-s22.text: For paths, a normalization step Npath(·) preserves structural delimiters while replacing volatile numeric or hexadecimal substrings with shared placeholders (e.g., ⟨NUM⟩).

p6-s23.text: Numerical values (τ = NUM) are projected using a log-scaled transformation that preserves magnitude without allowing large values to dominate.

p10-s13.text: MeCoLog incorporates RoPE [18] to capture the relative temporal dependencies between log events, which are more critical for anomaly detection than absolute positioning.

p10-s14.text: Standard positional encodings often conflate positional and semantic signals by adding fixed offsets, making attention scores a function of absolute indices rather than relative distances.

p10-s15.text: This is insufficient for log sequences, where anomalous executions typically manifest as violated ordering constraints or unexpected temporal gaps, signals that are defined by the distance between events rather than their specific positions in a window.

p10-s16.text: By applying RoPE directly to the query and augmented key projections, the model encodes position by rotating vectors in a multi-dimensional complex space.

p10-s17.text: This ensures that the dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n depends solely on the relative offset (m – n), allowing the Transformer to focus on the sequential flow of the system state.

p11-s9.text: We formulate cross-system log anomaly detection as a few-shot metric-learning problem under the episodic meta-learning paradigm [28,29].

p11-s10.text: Training tasks are sampled from a distribution p(T ) of episodic tasks constructed from the source system.

p11-s11.text: Each task Ti is a N-way K-shot episode: N classes (normal and one or many anomaly classes), each represented by K support samples.

p11-s13.text: • A support set S = Snorm ∪Sanom, where |Snorm| = |Sanom| = K.

p11-s14.text: This simulates the few-shot calibration available at deployment.

p11-s15.text: Snorm and Sanom are the support sets of normal and anomalous sequences respectively

p11-s16.text: • A query set Q, drawn from the same system but disjoint from S, used to compute the training loss.

p11-s17.text: The value of K is varied across experiments to assess sensitivity to support set size.

p11-s18.text: During meta-training the model parameters ϕ are updated so that performance on Q improves after conditioning on S.

p11-s19.text: During meta-testing on a new target system, only a small labeled support set is available; the model reuses the transferable embedding learned from source systems and calibrates the detection boundary on the fly without any retraining.

p11-s20.text: The episodic procedure directly mirrors the target deployment scenario.

p11-s21.text: By training on diverse episodic tasks sampled from the source system, the model learns a general adaptation strategy rather than source-specific patterns.

p11-s22.text: This means no distributional alignment between source and target systems is assumed or required.

p11-s23.text: The model learns how to adapt, not what the target looks like.

p11-s25.text: Standard supervised contrastive objectives treat all classes symmetrically, which is appropriate only when all classes are equally compact.

p11-s26.text: Log anomaly detection violates this assumption: normal behaviors are semantically stable and form compact clusters, whereas anomalies arise from diverse, unpredictable causes.

p11-s27.text: A symmetric loss imposes a false structural equivalence on these distinct data geometries.

p11-s28.text: We propose a loss that reflects this asymmetry directly.

p11-s29.text: Normal queries use standard prototype cross-entropy to tighten the normal cluster.

p11-s30.text: Anomaly queries use a margin-augmented variant that concentrates gradients on “hard” anomalies, namely those closest to the normal prototype.

p11-s31.text: It does not impose a compactness constraint on anomaly embeddings.

p11-s32.text: Our Asymmetric Prototype Contrastive Loss (APCL) inflates the normal prototype similarity for anomaly queries using an adaptive margin δ(zq) during training.

p12-s7.text: To separate anomalies from normal samples, we propose the Adaptive Margin Mechanism, which dynamically penalizes anomalies residing near the normal cluster.

p12-s8.text: The difficulty of an anomaly query za is quantified by its proximity to µnorm:

p12-s10.text: This formulation ensures that the margin grows proportionally to the proximity for hard anomalies, while remaining zero for anomalies already positioned in the opposite hemisphere.

p12-s11.text: For a query sample zq with label yq ∈{normal, abnormal}, let s(zq, µ) denote the scaled cosine similarity zq · µ/τ .

p12-s12.text: The margin-adjusted similarity to the normal prototype is defined as:

p12-s16.text: The APCL loss treats the normal and anomalous queries asymmetrically by inflating the denominator for anomalies.

p12-s17.text: The unified objective for a single query zq is expressed as:

p12-s18.text: LAPCL(zq, yq) = – log exp(s(zq, µyq)) exp(ˆs(zq, µnorm)) + exp(s(zq, µanom)) (13)

p12-s26.text: The APCL design shapes the embedding space by encouraging normal samples to form a compact cluster while allowing anomalies to remain diverse across different system contexts.

p12-s27.text: Anomaly queries are attracted toward an episode-local anomaly prototype through the numerator of Eq. 13.

p12-s28.text: However, APCL removes the symmetric same-class pairwise compaction of standard contrastive objectives, and the anomaly prototype is recomputed per episode from varying anomaly compositions.

p12-s29.text: No fixed global anomaly center therefore exists, and the adaptive margin concentrates the gradient on separating hard anomalies from the normal prototype rather than on compressing the anomaly class.

p12-s30.text: This design links training more closely to inference, since the adaptive margin δ(za) = max(0, 1 – Score(za)) assigns larger penalties to anomalies with higher inference risk.

p12-s31.text: As a result, training focuses more on hard anomalies, namely those with low Score(za) = 1 – za · µnorm, which are more likely to be confused with normal samples at test time.

p12-s32.text: This helps make the inference rule ˆy(xq) = arg maxc fϕ(xq) · µc more robust, without requiring manual threshold tuning or F1-based grid search.

p13-s8.text: We evaluate the performance of MeCoLog using four widely recognized benchmark datasets: HDFS [1], BGL [31], Thunderbird [31], and Hadoop [22].

p13-s9.text: Each dataset comprises raw log lines labeled as either normal or anomalous.

p13-s10.text: We process all datasets through a standardized pipeline of log parsing, template extraction, and sequence construction to ensure a fair and consistent comparison across all evaluated methods.

p13-s11.text: For the HDFS dataset, we employ session-based grouping via BlockID, whereas Hadoop, BGL and Thunderbird are processed using a sliding window approach with a window size and step size both set to 20.

p13-s12.text: Each system is split into training and testing partitions before any cross-domain experiment, with parameter vocabularies fit on the training partition only.

p13-s13.text: All datasets use an 80/20 train/test split.

p13-s14.text: For BGL and Thunderbird, a chronological split is used to preserve temporal ordering.

p13-s15.text: For HDFS and Hadoop, the split is performed randomly at the session/block level.

p13-s16.text: For cross-domain evaluation, MeCoLog meta-trains on the entire source training partition and evaluates exclusively on the target test partition.

p13-s17.text: The few-shot support set at inference is drawn from the target test pool.

p13-s18.text: Source test data and target training data are never used for model optimization.

p13-s22.text: Together, these characteristics quantify the structural gap between source and target systems, providing insight into the challenges of cross-system transfer.

p15-s5.text: To evaluate the effectiveness of MeCoLog, we compare it against two distinct groups of baseline models, ranging from classical single-system architectures to state-of-the-art cross-system methods.

p15-s6.text: Single-System Log Anomaly Detection Baselines: These models serve as benchmarks for assessing the fundamental discriminative power of log representations within a single domain:

p15-s7.text: • DeepLog [5]: A semi-supervised method using LSTMs to model system execution sequences as a language modeling task, flagging unexpected log key transitions.

p15-s8.text: • LogAnomaly [6]: An extension incorporating Word2Vec semantics to simultaneously capture sequential order and quantitative count-based deviations.

p15-s9.text: • LogRobust [9]: A supervised Bi-LSTM with attention engineered to handle template instability and noisy labels in realworld logs.

p15-s10.text: Cross-System and Few-Shot Learning Baselines: These methods explicitly address the challenges of domain shift and label scarcity in target systems:

p15-s11.text: • LogTransfer [10]: A supervised transfer learning approach that pre-trains an encoder on source data and fine-tunes the classifier on the target system.

p15-s12.text: • MetaLog [13]: A cross-system framework using a meta-learning strategy over source tasks to enable rapid target adaptation given a few-shot support set.

p15-s13.text: • LogTAD [12]: An unsupervised domain adaptation method that learns a unified representation space and measures distance from a global normal distribution.

p15-s14.text: • LogFormer [25]: A pre-training and adapter-based Transformer with character-level parameter encodings, whose twostage pipeline requires labeled data from both domains.

p15-s15.text: All baselines utilize their originally designed feature representations and published hyperparameter configurations, as reliable re-tuning is impractical given the strict few-shot budget of the target system.

p15-s16.text: The target few-shot support set (fixed at K = 20 per class, sharing identical query splits with MeCoLog) is applied via each baseline’s native adaptation mechanism.

p15-s17.text: For semi-supervised models (DeepLog, LogAnomaly), which lack mechanisms to train on anomalies, support anomalies are used solely to calibrate the decision threshold.

p15-s18.text: For supervised baselines (LogRobust, LogTransfer), the support samples are integrated into their respective training or fine-tuning procedures to ensure a consistent target-label budget across all evaluated methods.

p15-s20.text: Log anomaly detection is inherently class-imbalanced, since anomalous sequences constitute only a small fraction of the total data.

p15-s21.text: Relying solely on accuracy can therefore be misleading.

p15-s22.text: We therefore evaluate MeCoLog using the following comprehensive suite of metrics:

p15-s23.text: • Precision, Recall, and F1-score: We report the macro-averaged Precision and Recall to assess the model’s accuracy and completeness in identifying anomalies.

p15-s24.text: The F1-score, calculated as the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, serves as our primary metric for performance comparison.

p16-s1.text: • ROC-AUC: We include the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve to measure the model’s ability to distinguish between normal and anomalous classes across various decision boundaries.

p16-s3.text: We evaluate the cross-system adaptability of MeCoLog through one-to-one (1 →1) transfer experiments across all six representative transfer pairs within the BGL, HDFS, Thunderbird and Hadoop benchmark suite.

p16-s6.text: We also include a heterogeneous mixture pair (HDFS ↔ BGL) to test the model’s robustness under significant domain shifts.

p16-s7.text: This structured comparison allows us to assess whether semantic and structural patterns learned from a source system can be effectively projected onto a previously unseen target environment with minimal supervision.

p22-s7.text: In this section, we evaluate the impact of the temperature hyperparameter τ on the model’s discriminative performance.

p22-s8.text: The temperature parameter plays a critical role in contrastive learning by controlling the “hardness” of the distribution over negative samples.

p22-s9.text: We conduct a grid sweep with τ ∈{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} across two representative cross-system transfer pairs: HDFS → BGL and Thunderbird → BGL.

p22-s10.text: The results are illustrated in Fig 11.

p22-s11.text: As shown in the figure, both the F1-score and AUC exhibit a high sensitivity to the choice of τ .

p22-s12.text: We observe that lower temperature values (τ ≤0.1) yield the best results, with performance peaking at approximately τ = 0.05.

p22-s13.text: Specifically, in the HDFS → BGL scenario, the F1-score reaches its maximum of 0.886 at τ = 0.1, while the AUC remains robust at 0.946.

p22-s14.text: However, as τ increases beyond 0.2, there is a sharp decline in detection accuracy, particularly in the F1-score which drops significantly to approximately 0.75–0.77 at τ = 0.5.

p22-s15.text: This trend can be explained by the fact that a smaller temperature encourages the model to focus more on the most difficult negative samples (hard negatives), leading to a more compact and well-separated representation space.

p22-s16.text: Conversely, a larger τ tends to smooth the similarity distribution, causing the model to treat all samples equally and losing its ability to distinguish subtle anomalies from normal operational patterns.

p22-s17.text: These findings suggest that a sharper contrastive distribution is essential for maintaining high precision in cross-system anomaly detection tasks.

p23-s13.text: In terms of GPU memory, MeCoLog requires a moderate amount of resources.

p23-s14.text: Its ablation variants exhibit identical memory consumption, which indicates that Parameter Integration and RoPE introduce negligible overhead.

p23-s15.text: The higher inference latency relative to lightweight baselines such as LogRobust (0.056–0.061s) is directly attributable to model capacity.

p23-s16.text: MeCoLog’s 8.34M parameters, driven by the GKI mechanism, the CharCNN parameter encoder, and multi-head attention, provide richer representational capacity at the cost of higher per-sample latency.

p23-s17.text: This remains practical for log monitoring deployments, which are not typically sub-millisecond latency-critical.

p23-s18.text: Overall, despite having the largest parameter count among the evaluated methods, MeCoLog maintains efficient training and inference characteristics while providing strong cross-system generalization capability.

p23-s19.text: The throughput column contextualizes the per-sample latency.

p23-s20.text: Under batched operation, MeCoLog sustains approximately 1,800 windows per second, within the same order of magnitude as LogFormer (approximately 2,300 win/s).

p23-s21.text: Log­ Former’s slightly higher throughput reflects the absence of the parameter encoder and GKI path.

p23-s22.text: This corresponds to over 150 million windows per day on a single GPU.

p23-s23.text: The batch-1 latency in the Inference Latency column therefore does not constrain realistic monitoring deployments.

p24-s2.text: In this paper, we presented MeCoLog, a meta-contrastive learning method for few-shot cross-system log anomaly detection.

p24-s3.text: By integrating a Hybrid Parameter Embedding layer with a Gated Key Injection mechanism, MeCoLog effectively captures the rich contextual semantics of log messages.

p24-s4.text: Furthermore, the Asymmetric Prototypical Contrastive Learning (APCL) objective enables the model to align representations across disparate domains using only a handful of target samples, significantly reducing the manual labeling burden.

p24-s5.text: Extensive experiments across various real-world datasets (including HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, and AIT-LDS v2.0) demonstrate that MeCoLog consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in cross-system transfer tasks, maintaining high robustness and efficiency under extreme few-shot constraints.

p24-s6.text: Despite these strengths, MeCoLog requires at least a few labeled target anomalies during adaptation and assumes source training systems have sufficient anomaly coverage.

p24-s7.text: Additionally, our evaluation relies on standard benchmarks that may not fully capture the complexity of modern infrastructures.

p24-s8.text: For future work, we plan to extend MeCoLog into a multi-source meta-training framework and develop a zero-anomaly adaptation variant via one-class classification fallback.

p24-s9.text: We also aim to support online stream learning for real-time log shifts, evaluate the model on modern cloud and microservice environments, and explore the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance the semantic understanding ‌of rare failure modes.
